title: SAT-based bounded checking (CBMC)
description: CBMC unrolls C programs up to a bound and encodes the whole thing — program plus the negated property — as a SAT formula. If the formula is satisfiable, the satisfying assignment is a concrete bug trace. It finds buffer overflows, null derefs, and assertion failures in real C code, automatically.
method: Unroll loops k times; convert to static single assignment; encode as SAT; a satisfying assignment = bug trace up to bound k.
usage: Set the unwinding bound to cover your loops; treat SAT as 'bug found' and UNSAT as 'clean up to bound'.

demo.code:
print('CBMC: unroll k=10, encode 2.1M clauses')
print('SAT -> trace: buffer overflow at line 42 (input: n=11)')

title: Incremental SAT solving
description: Deepening the bound from k to k+1 shouldn't redo all the work: incremental SAT solvers keep learned clauses across runs, so each deeper check reuses the previous one's reasoning. Incremental BMC turns bound-deepening from quadratic into near-linear cost.
method: Solve under assumptions for bound k; add the k+1 layer as new clauses; re-solve reusing learned clauses; repeat.
usage: Use incremental mode when deepening; keep the solver session alive across bounds.

demo.code:
print('k=10 solved in 3.2s; k=11 reuses clauses -> 0.4s')
print('incremental deepening: 8x faster than fresh solves')

title: Witness validation and traces
description: A BMC 'bug found' is only useful if the trace replays: witness validation feeds the satisfying assignment back as concrete inputs and runs the actual program to confirm the violation. Validated witnesses become regression tests; unvalidated ones are just solver output.
method: Extract inputs from the model; execute concretely; confirm the violation; convert to a regression test.
usage: Always validate witnesses concretely before filing bugs; keep validated traces as tests.

demo.code:
print('witness: n=11 -> concrete run overflows at line 42: CONFIRMED')
print('trace saved as regression test')

title: BMC for concurrent programs
description: BMC handles concurrency by encoding thread interleavings up to a context-switch bound: the formula captures all schedules with at most k preemptions. Context-bounded checking finds the shallow concurrency bugs (races, deadlocks) that actually occur in practice, where bug depth is usually small.
method: Encode threads + scheduler with context-switch bound k; SAT finds violating schedules within the bound; deepen k incrementally.
usage: Start with small context bounds (2-3); most real concurrency bugs appear there.

demo.code: print('context bound 2: SAT -> data race (thread A write, thread B read, 1 preemption)')

title: Bounded checking of smart contracts
description: Smart contracts are ideal BMC targets: small, high-value, and bugs cost real money. Tools bound-check Solidity for reentrancy, integer issues, and access-control violations before deployment — when the code is immutable, the bound must be checked before it ships.
method: Translate contract to a checkable model; bound loops and call depth; check security properties; fix before deployment.
usage: Check every contract before mainnet; bound call depth and loops realistically.

demo.code:
print('contract Vault: reentrancy check, call-depth bound 3')
print('UNSAT -> no reentrancy within bound; deploy approved')

title: Industrial BMC deployment (hardware)
description: BMC's biggest wins are in hardware: Intel, IBM, and ARM use bounded model checking on chip designs, finding bugs in circuits with billions of states. The methodology — properties as assertions, bounded proofs in CI, bug traces to designers — is the template for BMC at industrial scale.
method: Embed assertions in RTL; run BMC in the design CI; triage traces with designers; track bound coverage per block.
usage: Start with critical blocks; grow bound coverage over time; make traces actionable for designers.

demo.code:
print('block FPU-div: 2,048 properties, bound 50, CI 12min')
print('0 violations -> tapeout gate passed')

title: Property-driven slicing
description: Most of a program is irrelevant to any one property. Slicing removes code that can't affect the checked property before encoding, shrinking the SAT formula dramatically. The slice is computed by dependency analysis from the property backwards — smaller formula, same verdict.
method: Backward slice from the property over data/control dependencies; encode only the slice; the verdict on the slice equals the verdict on the whole.
usage: Always slice before encoding; verify the slicer is sound for your language subset.

demo.code:
print('program: 12k lines; slice for property P: 340 lines')
print('formula 40x smaller, verdict identical')

title: Bit-precise memory modeling
description: BMC's power for C comes from bit-precise modeling: every integer is its actual bitvector, every pointer an address into a modeled heap. Overflows, sign errors, and pointer arithmetic bugs that abstract analyses miss are exactly what bit-blasting catches — the model matches the machine.
method: Model memory as arrays of bitvectors; pointer ops become address arithmetic; the SAT encoding captures wraparound and aliasing precisely.
usage: Rely on bit-precision for arithmetic-heavy code; abstract the heap where full precision explodes.

demo.code:
print('x = INT_MAX; x + 1 -> bitvector wraps to INT_MIN')
print('BMC flags signed overflow precisely (not heuristically)')
